new_statements.rule_in_words: Kolokuma Izon is a two-tone (H/L) language in which stress is non-contrastive and fully predictable from the tone pattern: stress falls on the first high tone of the compilation of high tones, on the first half of a phonetic falling tone, on the first half of a phonetic rising tone (except that when the first vowel is high and the second non-high the second half is stressed), and on the first syllable of a VV unit. Rhythm is described as neither syllable-timed nor stress-timed; tone groups occupy roughly equal time intervals.

new_statements.exceptions: Rule (c) has a segmental exception: in a rising tone whose first vowel is high and second vowel non-high, stress moves to the second part (ndaá 'but', anjá 'so, then').
new_statements.domain_note: Examples are single words (bird, sweat, 'but', 'so, then', an interrogative emphasizer), but the rules refer to phonetic tone sequences, which in Kolokuma are set at the level of the tone group/breath group (the passage follows the intonation section, and the preceding snippet text is about breath groups ending in low tones); stress is thus a phrase-level correlate of the tonal melody rather than a lexical word property. Source describes the Kolokuma dialect (kolo1262) only; Jenewari 1989 notes that Kolokuma and Mein are two-tone while Nembe and many Southern Izon dialects (Bumo, Arogbo) are 'accent' systems with one basic high per phrase, so this statement should not be extended to Bumo or other Izon dialects without Efere 2001.
new_statements.identity_note: The statement describes the Kolokuma dialect of Izon (Glottolog dialect kolo1262 'Kolokuma-Opokuma', under izon1238), a two-tone (H/L) dialect. Other Izon dialects (Bumo bumo1235, Arogbo) are described by Jenewari 1989 and Efere 2001 as pitch accent systems with one basic high per phrase; the Kolokuma stress-from-tone rule should be tagged as dialect-specific. The secondary Ndimele & Efere snippet ('Bumo.. is essentially pitch accent') refers to bumo1235.

tone_statements.quote: This paper establishes the lexical tone contrasts in the Nigerian language Izon, focusing on evidence for floating tone. Many tonal languages show effects of floating tone, though typically in a restricted way, such as occurring with only a minority of morphemes, or restricted to certain grammatical enviromnents. For Izon, the claim here is that all lexical items sponsor floating tone, making it ubiquitous across the lexicon and as common as pre-associated tone. The motivation for floating tone comes from the tonal patterns of morphemes in isolation and within tone groups.

readall_conflicts: No two sources disagree about the same variety. Williamson 1965 describes Kolokuma as a two-tone language with fully predictable, tone-driven stress (first of the compilation of high tones, etc.). Efere 2001 describes Bumo as a pitch accent system with at most one underlying H per word and gives no phonetic stress rule; Efere himself frames this as a dialect split inside Izon (Kolokuma and Kalabari tonal, Nembe and Bumo pitch accent, following Williamson 1978 on a drift from tone to pitch accent). Secondary sources seen in snippets agree with that split (Jenewari 1989: Kolokuma and Mein two tones without downstep, Bumo and Arogbo one basic high tone per phrase; Hyman 2018 on Efere's four Bumo word classes A-D, class A unaccented). So the catalog's dialect-unspecified 'Izon' record rests on Kolokuma; a Bumo entry would read pitch accent.

sources.citation: Rolle, Nicholas. 2021. Lexical tone contrast in Izon as ubiquitous floating tone. Phonological Data and Analysis 3(4): 1-40.
sources.quote: This paper establishes the lexical tone contrasts in the Nigerian language Izon, focusing on evidence for floating tone. Many tonal languages show effects of floating tone, though typically in a restricted way, such as occurring with only a minority of morphemes, or restricted to certain grammatical enviromnents. For Izon, the claim here is that all lexical items sponsor floating tone, making it ubiquitous across the lexicon and as common as pre-associated tone. The motivation for floating tone comes from the tonal patterns of morphemes in isolation and within tone groups.
sources.locator: abstract, Cambridge Core landing page of DOI 10.3765/pda.v3art4.37
sources.note: Establishes the lexical tone contrasts of Izon with two tone levels plus floating tones; argues every lexical morpheme sponsors a floating tone and sorts all lexical morphemes into four tone classes A-D by the floating tone(s) they end in, motivated by isolation patterns and behaviour inside tone groups; discusses OCP(T) violations and the coincidence of word-initial vowels with L tone.
